opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of those things where people tend to frame it as a fundamental barrier, and I'm not sure it is. My view has been that there are a few different paths, and we don't necessarily need to solve "continual learning" in the classic sense to get most of the value.

The first path is that it may matter less than people think. These models already have an enormous amount of general knowledge from pre-training and RL. A lot of what a human learns on the job is context: who's who, how this codebase is structured, what the customer cares about. A surprising amount of that can be handled in context. Context windows have gotten very long, and models are getting better at using them. If you can give a model a million tokens of everything relevant about your company, plus a good memory system, that covers a lot of what we call "learning on the job."

The second path is that you can do it more directly. There's no law of nature saying you can't update weights based on deployment experience. There are engineering challenges: how do you do it safely, how do you avoid the model drifting or picking up bad behaviors, how do you do it per customer without mixing data. But those feel like problems that yield to effort, not deep conceptual walls. We've seen this pattern over and over. Someone says "models can't do X, that's the fundamental limitation," and then a year or two later X just kind of falls out of scaling plus some fairly ordinary engineering.

So I'd put it this way: I don't think continual learning is the thing that stands between us and very powerful AI. It's one of several capabilities that will probably get solved incrementally, partly through longer context and better memory, partly through actual training-time approaches. Even if it were never fully solved, I think you'd still get models that can do most of the economically valuable work of a very capable professional, because so much of that is general skill plus reading the situation, and models are already quite good at both.

Where I'd be more humble is on timing and on the safety side. A model that keeps changing after deployment is a harder thing to evaluate and to trust. So I think the interesting question isn't really "can we do it," it's "how do we do it so we still understand what the model is and what it's going to do."

r001.rationale: The response discusses incremental progress but expresses humility about timing and does not estimate a good chance of solving continual learning within one or two years.

r002.rationale: It says models could do most economically valuable work without continual learning, but does not state that this could support a market worth trillions annually.

r003.rationale: It proposes using longer context windows, alongside a memory system, to cover much of what is called learning on the job.

r004.rationale: It calls direct weight-update challenges engineering problems, but does not characterize obstacles to making longer contexts work that way.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the places where I'm actually a bit more optimistic than some people, and also a bit less sure that it matters as much as everyone thinks.

Let me take the second part first. There's this view that continual learning is the missing piece, that models are frozen after training and a human employee learns on the job, so until we solve that, the models will never really be able to do a job. And I understand the intuition. But I think it undersells how far you can get with what we already have. The context window keeps getting longer, retrieval keeps getting better, and you can give a model a lot of the scaffolding of "learning" by just letting it read what happened yesterday. We've seen this in our own deployments. A model that has access to a codebase, the commit history, the previous conversations, a set of notes it wrote itself, that model behaves in a way that looks a lot like someone who's been on the team for a few months. It's not weight updates, but from the outside it's hard to tell the difference, and I'm not sure the user cares about the mechanism.

Now, is that the same thing as true continual learning? No. There's a real distinction between having information in context and having it baked into the model's intuitions. A human who's done a job for five years isn't just recalling facts, they've reshaped how they perceive the problem. And the honest answer is we don't have a clean way to do that yet without running into the problems people have known about for decades, catastrophic forgetting, the model getting worse at the general stuff as it specializes. There are approaches, lightweight fine-tuning, various forms of memory architectures, and I think some of them will work. I'd be surprised if this is still a major unsolved problem in two or three years. It just doesn't feel to me like it requires a fundamental conceptual breakthrough. It feels like the kind of thing that gets solved by a lot of engineering and a lot of compute, which is the kind of thing that historically does get solved.

But I want to flag the part that I actually worry about, which is less whether we can do it and more what happens when we do. A model that's frozen is a model you can evaluate. You test it, you understand its behavior, you deploy it, and it's the same thing on Tuesday that it was on Monday. Once models are updating themselves based on their experience in the world, you've got millions of slightly different models, and each one has been shaped by data you didn't curate. That's a safety problem and it's a security problem. Someone can poison what a model learns. A model can drift in ways nobody intended and nobody notices for a while. So I think of continual learning less as a capability we're racing toward and more as a capability where I want the control and interpretability tools to be ready before it becomes the default. We've talked about interpretability as an MRI for the model. Well, if the patient is changing every day, you'd better have a very fast MRI.

So, prospects: I think it's coming, I think it's maybe less of a bottleneck than people assume because of the context window substitutes, and I think the hard part isn't making it work, it's making it work in a way where we still understand what we've built.

r001.rationale: The response expects the problem may be solved in two or three years, not within the next one or two years.

r002.rationale: It does not state that AI could support a market worth trillions of dollars annually without continual learning.

r003.rationale: It presents longer context windows as a substitute for learning on the job, allowing models to read prior events and notes.

r004.rationale: It describes true continual learning as an engineering challenge, but does not characterize obstacles to making longer context windows work.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to separate two questions. One is whether a model can learn something over the course of doing a task. You give it feedback, it tries a different approach, and it carries that information forward in its context. The other is whether that experience produces a durable improvement that transfers to the next task, or to the next person using the model. Those are different capabilities.

For the second one, the challenge is deciding what to learn from. If a model tries something and the user says, “Great,” does that mean it was correct? Does it mean it was useful in that particular situation? Should you change the model’s general behavior as a result? You need a way to turn experience into a reliable learning signal without teaching the system the wrong lessons.

I’m optimistic that we can make progress there. I don’t see a fundamental reason models couldn’t learn continually. But I’m less certain about when we’ll have systems that do it reliably across a very broad range of work.

And I wouldn’t assume that everything has to wait for that. A model can get quite far by having strong general capabilities, access to the relevant information, and enough context to adapt to the task. Continual learning would make those systems more useful, especially in jobs where there’s a lot of accumulated, implicit knowledge. The interesting question is how much of that adaptation requires changing the model itself, and how much can happen through memory and context.

r001.rationale: The response is optimistic about progress but says it is uncertain when reliable continual learning across broad work will arrive; it gives no one-to-two-year estimate.

r002.rationale: It does not state that AI could support a market worth trillions of dollars annually without continual learning.

r003.rationale: It mentions using context to adapt to a task, but does not propose extending model context length.

r004.rationale: It does not characterize the obstacles to longer contexts as engineering problems; its statement about no fundamental reason applies to continual learning generally.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two different questions here. One is whether a model can adapt within the context of doing a task: you give it feedback, it sees what went wrong, and it adjusts. The other is whether that experience produces a durable improvement that carries over to the next task or the next customer. Those are different capabilities.

For the second, you need more than a mechanism for updating the model. You need to figure out which experiences contain a useful lesson, whether the feedback is reliable, and whether learning that lesson damages something the model already knows. In a workplace, success can also be ambiguous. Someone approving your answer doesn’t necessarily mean you did the job correctly.

My guess is that we’ll see this happen in stages. You can start with memory, then collect experience and use it to train subsequent versions, and eventually make that process more immediate. It doesn’t have to be a system that updates its weights after every interaction.

The thing I’d watch is whether a model gets reliably better at a particular job over weeks of doing it, with less human intervention. That would be a much stronger demonstration than just showing that it can incorporate a correction in a conversation.

r001.rationale: The candidate predicts staged progress but gives no estimate that continual on-the-job learning has a good chance of being solved within one or two years.

r002.rationale: It does not state that AI could support a market worth trillions of dollars annually without continual learning.

r003.rationale: It mentions memory and learning across tasks, but does not propose extending model context length.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss longer-context obstacles or characterize them as engineering problems rather than fundamental limitations.
